title: Abena and the Beginning of Everything

pages.text: As dusk settled over the green hills of Kuntunse near Accra, thirteen-year-old Abena tilted her head back. Above her stood the giant white dish of the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory, thirty-two metres wide, pointing silently toward the first bright stars.
sentences: As dusk settled over the green hills of Kuntunse near Accra, thirteen-year-old Abena tilted her head back.
Above her stood the giant white dish of the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory, thirty-two metres wide, pointing silently toward the first bright stars.
pages.alt: Abena and Kwame stand with Dr Mensah at dusk before the giant white thirty-two-metre radio telescope dish at Kuntunse.

pages.text: ‘Dr Mensah,’ Abena asked, opening her yellow notebook, ‘our textbook says the universe began with the Big Bang. When I hear those words, I picture a giant bomb exploding in the middle of an empty dark room. Is that what happened?’
sentences: ‘Dr Mensah,’ Abena asked, opening her yellow notebook, ‘our textbook says the universe began with the Big Bang.
When I hear those words, I picture a giant bomb exploding in the middle of an empty dark room.
Is that what happened?’
pages.alt: Abena holds open her yellow notebook and asks Dr Mensah a question while Kwame listens.

pages.text: Dr Mensah smiled and shook his head gently. ‘That is the most common misunderstanding in astronomy, Abena. The Big Bang was not an explosion from one point into empty space that was already sitting there. Before it, there was no empty room waiting outside. Instead, space itself began to expand everywhere at once.’
sentences: Dr Mensah smiled and shook his head gently.
‘That is the most common misunderstanding in astronomy, Abena.
The Big Bang was not an explosion from one point into empty space that was already sitting there.
Before it, there was no empty room waiting outside.
Instead, space itself began to expand everywhere at once.’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah gestures with both hands to explain that space itself expands everywhere, while Abena and Kwame listen intently.

pages.text: He picked up a loaf of uncut raisin bread from the snack table. ‘Imagine unbaked dough with raisins mixed all through it,’ he said. ‘As the dough rises, every raisin moves farther from every other raisin, not because the raisins are flying through the dough, but because the dough between them is stretching.’
sentences: He picked up a loaf of uncut raisin bread from the snack table.
‘Imagine unbaked dough with raisins mixed all through it,’ he said.
‘As the dough rises, every raisin moves farther from every other raisin, not because the raisins are flying through the dough, but because the dough between them is stretching.’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah holds a loaf of raisin bread at a table, pointing out how raisins sit inside the dough.

pages.text: ‘In our universe,’ Dr Mensah continued, ‘the raisins are like galaxies, vast islands of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Our own home galaxy, the Milky Way, is one of them. Gravity keeps each galaxy together so it does not stretch, while the space between distant galaxies keeps expanding.’
sentences: ‘In our universe,’ Dr Mensah continued, ‘the raisins are like galaxies, vast islands of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
Our own home galaxy, the Milky Way, is one of them.
Gravity keeps each galaxy together so it does not stretch, while the space between distant galaxies keeps expanding.’
pages.alt: A glowing visual model on a screen shows spiral galaxies in deep space moving apart as the grid of space stretches between them.

pages.text: Kwame raised his hand. ‘How do scientists know space is really stretching? Nobody was there billions of years ago to watch!’ Dr Mensah nodded. ‘Science relies on evidence we can measure today. First, when we study light from distant galaxies, we see that the light waves have been stretched toward the red end of the spectrum.’
sentences: Kwame raised his hand.
‘How do scientists know space is really stretching?
Nobody was there billions of years ago to watch!’ Dr Mensah nodded.
‘Science relies on evidence we can measure today.
First, when we study light from distant galaxies, we see that the light waves have been stretched toward the red end of the spectrum.’
pages.alt: Kwame raises his hand beside Abena while Dr Mensah shows a colourful rainbow prism spectrum and stretched light waves.

pages.text: ‘We call this redshift,’ said Dr Mensah. ‘In the nineteen-twenties, astronomers discovered that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is stretched and the faster it recedes from us. If galaxies are moving apart today, then running the cosmic film backward tells us they were much closer together in the past.’
sentences: ‘We call this redshift,’ said Dr Mensah.
‘In the nineteen-twenties, astronomers discovered that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is stretched and the faster it recedes from us.
If galaxies are moving apart today, then running the cosmic film backward tells us they were much closer together in the past.’
pages.alt: Abena draws wavy lines in her yellow notebook showing short blue waves stretching into longer red waves.

pages.text: ‘Is redshift the only clue?’ asked Abena. ‘No,’ said Dr Mensah, pointing up at the Kuntunse dish. ‘In the early universe, about thirteen point eight billion years ago, everything was an extremely hot, dense sea of particles and light. As space expanded, that sea cooled down.’
sentences: ‘Is redshift the only clue?’ asked Abena.
‘No,’ said Dr Mensah, pointing up at the Kuntunse dish.
‘In the early universe, about thirteen point eight billion years ago, everything was an extremely hot, dense sea of particles and light.
As space expanded, that sea cooled down.’
pages.alt: Through the window, the giant white Kuntunse radio telescope dish gleams against a deep indigo sky filled with stars.

pages.text: ‘After about three hundred and eighty thousand years,’ Dr Mensah explained, ‘the universe cooled enough for atoms of hydrogen and helium to form. Light could finally travel freely through space. Today, radio telescopes still detect that ancient, cooled afterglow coming from every direction in the sky. We call it the Cosmic Microwave Background.’
sentences: ‘After about three hundred and eighty thousand years,’ Dr Mensah explained, ‘the universe cooled enough for atoms of hydrogen and helium to form.
Light could finally travel freely through space.
Today, radio telescopes still detect that ancient, cooled afterglow coming from every direction in the sky.
We call it the Cosmic Microwave Background.’
pages.alt: An all-sky oval map of soft golden and blue speckles glows on a monitor as Abena and Kwame study it in wonder.

pages.text: ‘Over hundreds of millions of years, gravity pulled clouds of that hydrogen and helium together to ignite the first stars,’ said Dr Mensah. ‘Inside their fiery cores, stars forged heavier elements like carbon, oxygen and iron. Every atom of iron in your blood was once forged inside an ancient star.’
sentences: ‘Over hundreds of millions of years, gravity pulled clouds of that hydrogen and helium together to ignite the first stars,’ said Dr Mensah.
‘Inside their fiery cores, stars forged heavier elements like carbon, oxygen and iron.
Every atom of iron in your blood was once forged inside an ancient star.’
pages.alt: Abena looks down at her own hand in amazement while a glowing star nursery nebula shines on the screen behind her.

pages.text: ‘Can our telescopes see the whole universe?’ Kwame asked. ‘Only the observable universe,’ Dr Mensah replied. ‘Because light takes time to travel, we can only see regions whose light has had time to reach Earth since the Big Bang. And as for the very first instant—what sparked the expansion, or what dark matter and dark energy truly are—those remain open questions.’
sentences: ‘Can our telescopes see the whole universe?’ Kwame asked.
‘Only the observable universe,’ Dr Mensah replied.
‘Because light takes time to travel, we can only see regions whose light has had time to reach Earth since the Big Bang.
And as for the very first instant—what sparked the expansion, or what dark matter and dark energy truly are—those remain open questions.’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah, Abena and Kwame look through a small optical telescope on the terrace under a vast starry sky.

pages.text: Abena closed her yellow notebook and looked up at the Milky Way arching over Kuntunse. Science was not a book of finished answers; it was a growing map built from careful evidence. ‘Good,’ she said with a smile. ‘That means there is still plenty left for us to discover.’ The end.

pages.alt: Abena smiles up at the glowing Milky Way above the Kuntunse radio telescope dish, holding her yellow notebook to her chest.

activities.question: Why is picturing the Big Bang as a bomb exploding in an empty room inaccurate?
options: Space itself expanded everywhere rather than matter exploding into empty space
The explosion happened inside a single giant star
The universe has always stayed the exact same size
activities.explanation: The Big Bang was the rapid expansion of space itself everywhere, not an explosion into pre-existing empty space.

activities.definition: Vast systems of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
distractors: Small rocks that burn up in Earth’s atmosphere
Instruments used to measure air temperature

activities.question: What does the redshift of light from distant galaxies show scientists?
options: Light waves stretch as space expands, showing distant galaxies are moving apart
Distant galaxies are painted red by interstellar dust
All galaxies are rushing toward the Milky Way
activities.explanation: As space expands, light waves travelling across it are stretched toward the red end of the spectrum.

activities.question: What is the Cosmic Microwave Background that radio telescopes detect?
options: The cooled afterglow light from the early hot universe
Signals sent by microwave ovens on Earth
Light reflected from the surface of the Moon
activities.explanation: It is the cooled remnant radiation from when the early universe first became transparent to light.

activities.question: Which of these is still an unresolved question in cosmology today?
options: What happened at the very earliest instant and what dark energy truly is
Whether light takes time to travel through space
Whether the Milky Way is a galaxy
activities.explanation: While expansion from an early hot, dense state is strongly supported, the very first instant and dark energy remain open research questions.

activities.prompt: Why is it important for scientists to separate well-tested evidence from questions that are not yet solved?
Put these cosmic events in order from earliest to latest.
items: The early universe expands from an extremely hot, dense state.
The universe cools enough for hydrogen and helium atoms to form.
Gravity pulls gas clouds together to ignite the first stars.
Stars forge heavier elements like carbon, oxygen and iron.

activities.prompt: How does learning about the size and history of the universe make you feel about asking big questions?

glossary.definition: A place with special telescopes used to study the sky and space.
To grow larger or stretch out over a wider space.
Vast islands of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
The natural force of attraction that pulls objects with mass toward one another.
The stretching of light waves toward the red end of the spectrum as space expands.
Basic building-block substances of matter, such as hydrogen, carbon and iron.
Able to be seen or detected; the observable universe is the part whose light has reached us.
